title: Rumors and Quorums
setting: a night wholesale produce market where news travels stall to stall

post.author: u/forklift_witold
post.title: I drive a forklift at a night produce market. At 00:40 our office recalled spinach lot 7714. At 03:15 a buyer's scanner called it clean, and I was loading it into his van.

blocks.text: I'm Witold, forklift driver on nights at the wholesale produce market. Fruit and veg leave by the pallet from midnight. News here travels stall to stall: one stall tells two more, they each tell two, and soon the whole hall knows.

Our stock book, the record of every pallet, lives on servers: computers that store records and answer questions. Each record lives on three, its home servers, each holding a home copy. Lot 7714's are A, B and C.

Saving a change is a write; it counts once 2 home copies say yes within 2 seconds. A buyer's scanner asking about a pallet makes a read; it takes the first 2 answers, and B and C, in the main hall, beat A, across the yard. Two plus two beats three, so a read should always meet the latest write.

The servers track each other by gossip, like the stalls: every second each tells one other, picked at random, what it knows, and news reaches all of them in about 2 seconds. If one goes quiet, another asks it directly, then asks others to try; still nothing, it's marked suspect, and after 5 more silent seconds, dead.

A dead home server can't say yes, so the market rents a stand-in, D. When fewer than 2 home copies answer a write in time, D says yes too and keeps a note: this belongs to C. When gossip says C is back, D hands it over. Only servers called dead get notes.

On Thursday 8 October our IT firm added a cost rule: remove a stand-in after 30 minutes with no writes. Before, it stayed until every note was handed over. Tonight was the first home server down since.

Thursday night, 15 October: C went down at 00:30 for an upgrade, until 02:00. At 00:28 the spinach's packer emailed a recall: listeria, a dangerous germ, on spinach lot 7714. At 00:40 Ngaire, our night manager, set a recall flag, a safety flag every scanner checks. Her screen said SAVED. She read it out on the market radio.

B was busy too: from 00:35 to 01:02 it was compacting, rewriting its stored files to free space, which makes it slow. A server drops any write it can't store before the 2-second deadline. Gossip called B alive, so nobody kept notes for it. From 00:35 to 01:00 writes landed on A and D; then A and B answered everything, and D sat idle.
Each line of the stock book's log: the time, the event, the servers.

00:30:08  C dead; stand-in D rented
00:40:00  write lot 7714 flag: yes A, D (note for C); B missed; SAVED
01:00:00  write: yes A, D (note for C); D's last
01:30:00  D removed, idle 30 min, 6 notes undelivered
02:00:00  C back
03:15:00  read lot 7714: B, C; CLEAN
Two servers said recalled. The two that answered at 03:15 had never heard.

At 03:15 I was loading Mr Pennycuick's van for his greengrocers. He scanned each pallet, and his scanner beeped green. Under my forklift's lights I read the label: lot 7714, the one from the radio at 00:41. I set it down and called Ngaire.

diagram.aria: The night from 00:30 to 03:30, one row per server. Amber is up without the recall flag, green holds it, red is B compacting and dropping writes. A holds the flag from 00:40. B compacts from 00:35 to 01:02 and never holds the flag. C is down from 00:30 to 02:00 and never holds the flag. Stand-in D holds the flag in its note for C from 00:40 until it is removed at 01:30. Markers: the flag saved on A and D at 00:40, D's last write at 01:00, D removed at 01:30, C back at 02:00, the scan reading clean at 03:15.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the stock book's log, Thursday 15 to Friday 16 October 2026. Green is a server holding the recall flag. Only A and stand-in D ever held it, and D was removed at 01:30 with its note for C. The 03:15 read took the first two answers, B and C.

blocks.text: We found every pallet of 7714 by hand before 04:00. Next Thursday, B gets its upgrade. What should we change before then?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Make two lists. The 00:40 write: which servers said yes, and which of those are lot 7714's home servers? The 03:15 read: which servers answered? Now find a server on both lists. Counting a stand-in's yes as if it were a home copy's is called a sloppy quorum, a quorum being the count of yeses that must agree. And where was the flag's note at 02:00?

replies.author: u/forklift_witold
replies.text: Write: A and D, and only A is a home server. Read: B and C. No server on both lists. The note was gone: D was removed at 01:30 holding it and 5 more for C.

comments.author: u/quorum_maths_hieronim
comments.text: Two copies to write plus two to read is more than three copies, so a read always sees the last write. That's arithmetic, and arithmetic doesn't break. What broke is who knew what, and when. Your servers learn who's up by gossip once a second, and at 03:15 the read trusted servers it had been told were fine. Make the servers gossip ten times as often, so news of a down server spreads faster.

replies.author: u/forklift_witold
replies.text: The IT firm likes it: one setting, no new servers.

comments.author: u/nearest_copy_pallavi
comments.text: At 03:15 the queue is at the loading bay, not in the servers. Let each scanner read the single nearest copy, B for the main hall, and buyers stop waiting for a second answer.

reply.prompt: Next Thursday B goes down for its upgrade. What should the market change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Make the servers gossip ten times as often, so news of a down server spreads faster.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October the IT firm set gossip to every tenth of a second. In the sim, replaying 15 October: C is declared dead 5.3 seconds after it stops instead of 8. Nothing else moves. The 00:40 write still counts A and D, D is still removed at 01:30 with its 6 notes for C, and the 03:15 read on B and C still says clean. On 22 October B went down for its upgrade and the same pattern came back: price changes had vanished from the scanners by morning.
options.senior: Gossip decides how fast the servers learn who is up; it never decides which servers a write and a read land on. The 00:40 write was counted on A and a stand-in, and the 03:15 read asked B and C: those sets share nothing, whatever the news speed. Faster gossip also costs messages, and detecting a death still waits out the suspect timer. The flaw is the count, not the rumour.

options.text: Write and read all three copies of every record, so no read can ever miss a write.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October the IT firm set every write and every read to need all three home copies. In the sim, replaying 15 October: the 00:40 flag is refused, Ngaire's screen says NOT SAVED, and the office retries every 5 minutes; it is refused 16 times and saved at 02:00, when C is back, on A, B and C. The 03:15 read asks all three and says recalled. But 17 other writes are refused between 00:30 and 01:55. On 22 October, B's upgrade stopped every stock write for the same 90 minutes, and the stalls wrote their sales on paper until 02:00.
options.senior: Needing every copy for both write and read gives a read that can never miss, and the price is availability: any one server down, slow or upgrading stops all writes to every record it holds. That is the honest trade-off, and some records deserve it. A market that runs on three servers will have one down most weeks, so this turns each upgrade into an outage. Two of three home copies already overlap; the bug was counting a stand-in.

options.text: Read each record from the nearest single copy, so a buyer's scanner answers faster.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October each scanner was set to ask one copy, the nearest: B for the main hall. In the sim, replaying 15 October: the 03:15 read asks B alone, and B dropped the flag while compacting, so the scan says clean. The waits at the loading bay were a little shorter. On 22 October B was the server being upgraded, so the scanners asked C, and every write C had missed during its own upgrade the week before read as if it had never happened.
options.senior: One copy for a read plus two for a write is three, not more than three, so a read can miss the latest write even with no stand-in at all; asking one copy gives up the overlap entirely. It is fine for things where old is harmless, like a stall's opening hours. A safety flag is the opposite: it must be found by every read, so it needs reads and writes that are sure to overlap.

options.text: Count a safety flag only when 2 of its 3 home copies hold it, not a stand-in.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October the IT firm changed three things. Safety flags now count only home copies. The cost rule removes a stand-in only after every note is handed over. And a tree repair compares the home copies every hour at half past and copies across anything missing. In the sim, replaying 15 October: at 00:40 only A says yes in time, so Ngaire's screen says NOT SAVED; she keeps the recall on the radio and the office retries every 5 minutes. It is saved at 01:05 on A and B, once B has finished compacting. D hands its 5 notes to C at 02:00:02 and is removed. The 02:30 repair copies the flag to C. At 03:15 the read asks B and C, and both say recalled. On 22 October B's upgrade came and went, and every flag the office set read back on every scanner.
options.senior: Two of three home copies for a write and two for a read must share a server, because the two sets of home servers overlap; that promise holds only when every yes comes from a home copy. So count safety flags strictly, and accept that a flag can be refused while two home servers are down or slow: a loud NOT SAVED is a problem a person can act on, a quiet SAVED is not. Keep stand-ins for everyday writes, but never remove one with notes still on it, and run a regular tree repair, because notes are best effort and a stand-in can still fail.

sim.title: Replay lot 7714's night
sim.lede: You're Witold's IT firm on the night of Thursday 15 October 2026, at 00:30, as C stops for its upgrade. As given data: lot 7714 lives on home servers A, B and C. A stock write lands on these three every 5 minutes from 00:30 to 03:30; the 00:40 one is the recall flag. A write counts once 2 copies say yes within 2 seconds; a read takes the first 2 answers, B and C before A. C is down from 00:30 to 02:00. B compacts from 00:35 to 01:02 and drops every write it can't store in time. Every second each server probes one other and gossips what it knows; a silent server is suspect, dead 5 seconds later, and the news reaches all in 2 rounds, so C is declared dead at 00:30:08. Then stand-in D is rented: it says yes when fewer than 2 home copies answer, and keeps a note for C. The cost rule removes D after 30 minutes with no writes. A refused safety flag is retried every 5 minutes. Set C's downtime, B's compacting, how the flag is counted, the removal rule, a regular repair that compares the copies, the gossip interval and the read and write counts, then play 00:30 to 03:30.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built: the flag is saved on A and D, D is removed at 01:30 with 6 notes for C, and the 03:15 read on B and C says clean. Count safety flags on home copies only: NOT SAVED at 00:40, saved at 01:05 on A and B, recalled at 03:15. Keep D until its notes are handed over: C gets the flag at 02:00:02. Repair every hour at half past: B gets it at 01:30. All three copies: 17 other writes refused, the flag saved at 02:00. The nearest single copy: B alone, clean. Gossip ten times as often: C dead after 5.3 s, still clean. Turn off B's compacting: the flag lands on A and B, and nothing is lost.

explain.oneLine: No server lost the recall. The 00:40 write counted a stand-in's yes, the stand-in was removed before it could hand its note to C, and the 03:15 read asked B and C, two servers that never took that write. Two plus two beats three only among home copies.

steps.title: Gossip and SWIM: how the servers knew C was down.
steps.text: Gossip spreads news like the stalls do. First, every second, each server picks one other at random and tells it everything it knows. Second, that one does the same in the next round. Third, news doubles each round, so among four servers it reaches all of them in about 2 rounds, 2 seconds. Deciding who is dead uses SWIM, the way Consul's Serf library works, with the suspect stage from Silence Isn't Death. First, a server probes another directly. Second, with no answer, it asks others to probe it too. Third, still silent, it is marked suspect, and gossip says so. Fourth, after 5 more seconds with no reply, it is declared dead. On Thursday that took 8 seconds for C. What can go wrong: SWIM only notices silence. B was slow, not silent, so gossip kept calling it alive.

steps.title: A sloppy write, and a note for C.
steps.text: The textbooks call the number of copies N, the yeses a write needs W, and the answers a read takes R; the market's are 3, 2 and 2, as in Two Leaders. Home servers are the ones a record belongs to, as on The Ring. In steps, the 00:40 write: first, it went to A, B and C. Second, A said yes; B, compacting, missed the 2-second deadline and later dropped it; C was dead. Third, with only 1 home yes, the write also went to stand-in D, which said yes and kept a note for C. Fourth, 2 yeses: SAVED. Counting a stand-in's yes is a sloppy quorum; the note and its later delivery are hinted handoff. What can go wrong: the note exists only on D, and B, alive but slow, got no note at all.

steps.title: The cost rule, and a read that met nobody.
steps.text: Hinted handoff in steps: first, the stand-in keeps the write with a note naming the home server it belongs to. Second, it watches gossip for that server to come back. Third, it hands the write over. Fourth, only then may it delete it. Last week's cost rule cut in after step 1: D's last write was at 01:00, so at 01:30, 30 minutes idle, it was removed with 6 notes still on it. C came back at 02:00 with nothing to collect. At 03:15 the read took the first two answers, B and C, and neither had the flag. R + W > N promises that any 2 home copies share one with any other 2 home copies. A and D against B and C share nothing, because D is not a home copy. Read repair, which fixes copies a read finds disagreeing, could not help: B and C agreed.

steps.title: The fix: count home copies, hand over every note, repair on a timer.
steps.text: First, a safety flag counts only when 2 of its 3 home copies say yes. At 00:40 only A did, so the screen said NOT SAVED and the office retried every 5 minutes until A and B both said yes at 01:05. Any read of 2 home copies now meets A or B. Second, a stand-in is removed only after every note is handed over: D hands C its 5 notes at 02:00:02. Third, a regular tree repair finds what one copy lacks. It uses a Merkle tree, a summary of summaries: each record gets a short fingerprint; each branch gets a fingerprint of the fingerprints below it; the top one sums up the whole stock book. Two servers compare top fingerprints; if they match, nothing differs; if not, they compare the branches below and walk down only where they differ, sending just the missing records. Run every hour at half past, it gives C the flag at 02:30.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail.
steps.text: Gossip ten times as often makes C dead after 5.3 seconds instead of 8, but the write still lands on A and D and the read on B and C: clean. Writing and reading all three copies can never miss, but it refuses 17 other writes while C is down and saves the flag only at 02:00, when C is back; every upgrade becomes an outage. Reading the nearest single copy asks B alone, which dropped the flag: clean, faster. One read plus two writes is three, not more than three, so it never promised an overlap.

diagram.aria: The fix replayed for Thursday 15 October. At 00:40 the office sends the recall flag to A, which says yes. B, compacting, does not answer in time. With only 1 of 3 home copies, the office's screen says NOT SAVED and it retries. At 01:05 the retry reaches B, which says yes, and A already holds it: 2 of 3 home copies, SAVED. At 02:30 the tree repair copies the flag from A to C. At 03:15 the scanner reads C and B, and both say recalled. Outcome: the scan refuses lot 7714.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for 15 October. The flag is refused loudly at 00:40 with A alone, and saved at 01:05 once A and B, two home copies, hold it. The 02:30 tree repair gives C its copy, so the 03:15 read on B and C finds it twice. D, which still takes other writes, hands its 5 notes to C at 02:00:02 before it is removed (not drawn).

fix.title: The fix: safety flags count home copies only, stand-ins hand over before they go, and a tree repair runs every hour
fix.text: Keep the sloppy count for everyday stock writes, where a short gap is harmless, but count a safety flag only when 2 of its 3 home copies hold it. If they can't, the screen says NOT SAVED and the office retries every 5 minutes, keeping the recall on the radio and on paper until it says SAVED. Change the cost rule so a stand-in is removed only after it has handed over every note, then 30 minutes idle. Add a tree repair that compares every pair of home copies every hour at half past and copies across whatever one lacks: the backstop for notes that never arrive and writes a busy server dropped. Then alert on two things: any stand-in holding notes, and any refused safety flag.

limits: A strict count can refuse a flag. With two of three home servers down or slow at once, no safety flag can be saved until one returns; the market needs its paper and radio routine for those minutes.
Notes are best effort even with the new rule. If the stand-in's own disk fails before C is back, its notes are gone, and only the tree repair closes the gap, up to an hour later.

A tree repair costs work on every server it compares, and its interval is how long a copy can stay wrong. Hourly suits a stock book; records that change money or safety need the strict count, not a faster repair.

explain.seniorTake: R + W > N is a promise about home copies, and every shortcut that keeps writes flowing, a stand-in's yes, a dropped late write, a note that can be thrown away, quietly steps outside it. Decide per kind of record: everyday stock can take a sloppy count and catch up later; a recall or a payment needs a strict count that refuses loudly. Then treat repair as part of the design, not a cleanup: hinted handoff for speed, a Merkle-tree comparison on a timer as the backstop, and nothing allowed to delete data that is still owed to someone. Gossip and SWIM tell you who is up; they don't tell you whether your read can see your write.

realWorld.title: Dynamo, 2007: R + W > N, usually (3,2,2)
realWorld.text: The Dynamo paper says "Setting R and W such that R + W > N yields a quorum-like system." and "The common (N,R,W) configuration used by several instances of Dynamo is (3,2,2)." Those are the market's numbers. A quorum-like system is one where any read and any write share at least one copy.

realWorld.title: Dynamo: the sloppy quorum
realWorld.text: To keep writes working through failures, Dynamo says "all read and write operations are performed on the first N healthy nodes from the preference list", not always the record's own home servers. A node is one machine; the preference list is Dynamo's ordered list of servers for a record, home servers first. That is the market's stand-in, and why R + W > N stops covering every read.

realWorld.title: Dynamo: hinted handoff, with an A and a D
realWorld.text: By coincidence the paper's example uses the same letters: "The replica sent to D will have a hint in its metadata that suggests which node was the intended recipient of the replica", and "Upon detecting that A has recovered, D will attempt to deliver the replica to A." Only then, it says, "D may delete the object from its local store without decreasing the total number of replicas in the system." A replica is a copy; metadata is the label on it. The market's cost rule deleted first.

realWorld.title: Dynamo: Merkle trees as the backstop
realWorld.text: The paper names the failure the market hit: "hinted replicas become unavailable before they can be returned to the original replica node". Its answer is a regular comparison: "A Merkle tree is a hash tree where leaves are hashes of the values of individual keys." and "Merkle trees help in reducing the amount of data that needs to be transferred while checking for inconsistencies". A hash is a short fingerprint of data; a key is a record's name; a leaf is the bottom of the tree.

realWorld.title: Dynamo: gossip for membership
realWorld.text: "Each node contacts a peer chosen at random every second" to swap what it knows about who is in the group. A peer is another server of the same kind. That is the market's gossip interval.

realWorld.title: Cassandra, 2009: quorums and gossip
realWorld.text: Lakshman and Malik describe the same design at Facebook: "For writes, the system routes the requests to the replicas and waits for a quorum of replicas to acknowledge the completion of the writes." To acknowledge is to say yes. And: "Within the Cassandra system Gossip is not only used for membership but also to disseminate other system related control state." To disseminate is to spread.

realWorld.title: Consul: gossip runs the membership list
realWorld.text: HashiCorp's Consul docs say "Serf is a gossip protocol that Consul implements in datacenter operations." and "Consul uses it to manage membership and broadcast messages to the cluster." A cluster is the group of servers; a datacenter is a building of them; to broadcast is to send to all.

realWorld.title: Serf: SWIM's steps in practice
realWorld.text: Serf's own guide gives the steps the market's servers follow: "Failure detection is done by periodic random probing using a configurable interval." Then "An indirect probe asks a configurable number of random nodes to probe the same node," and a suspect node is declared dead "If the suspect member of the cluster does not dispute the suspicion within a configurable period of time,". Configurable means you set it; the market's are 1 second and 5 seconds.

realWorld.title: SWIM, 2002
realWorld.text: Serf's guide says "The gossip protocol is based on" the paper SWIM: Scalable Weakly-consistent Infection-style Process Group Membership Protocol, by Das, Gupta and Motivala, which Consul's Gossip page also links. Infection-style means news spreads from server to server the way a cold does.

asked: What does R + W > N guarantee, and when does it fail?
How do replicas find and repair differences?
interview.answer: With N copies of a record, a write that waits for W of them and a read that asks R of them must share at least one copy when R + W > N, so the read sees the write: with N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2, any two copies share one. That guarantee is only about the record's home copies. It fails when a system counts something else: a sloppy quorum, where a stand-in's yes counts while a home server is down; a write a slow copy drops after the deadline; or a read or write count that adds up to N or less. Hinted handoff is how a sloppy quorum pays its debt, in steps: the stand-in keeps the write with a note naming the home server it was meant for, watches the membership gossip for that server to come back, hands the write over, and only then deletes it. It is best effort: if the stand-in fails or is removed first, the note is lost. So replicas also need anti-entropy: a Merkle tree, a summary of summaries, where each record has a hash, each branch hashes the hashes below it, and two replicas compare top hashes and walk down only the branches that differ, sending just the missing records. Read repair fixes a copy a read finds out of date, but only if the read asked a copy that has the newer value. For a value that must be seen, such as a safety flag or a payment, I'd count only home copies and accept refused writes. I'd tell the story of a produce market whose recall flag was counted on one home server and a stand-in that was removed with its note, so a read on the other two home servers said clean.

terms.def: A market where growers and packers sell fruit and vegetables in bulk, by the pallet, to shops and restaurants. Witold's runs from midnight.
A flat wooden base that goods are stacked on, so a forklift can lift a whole load at once.
A batch of produce from one packing run, with one number on every pallet's label, so a recall can name exactly what to stop. Spinach lot 7714 is one.
A business that washes, packs and labels produce before it reaches the market. Lot 7714's packer tests its spinach and issued the recall.
An order to stop selling a product and bring it back because it may be unsafe. Lot 7714's packer emailed one to the market office at 00:28.
A germ found in some foods, such as leafy greens, that can make people seriously ill. A lab test found it on lot 7714.
The person in charge of the market overnight. Ngaire set the recall flag at 00:40 and read the recall out on the radio.
The two-way radios the market's staff carry. Ngaire read the recall out on it, and Witold heard it at 00:41.
A handheld reader a buyer points at a pallet's label. It reads the lot's record from the stock book and beeps green if it is clean.
The market's record of every pallet and lot, kept on servers A, B and C. Also called the tally.
A computer that stores records and answers questions about them for other machines, such as scanners.
One of the servers a record belongs to. Lot 7714's are A, B and C, and each holds a full home copy. Stand-ins are not home servers.
The copy of a record kept on one of its home servers. Lot 7714 has three.
Saving a change to a record. At the market a write counts once 2 home copies say yes within 2 seconds, or 1 home copy and a stand-in, as built.
Asking for a record's current value. A scanner's read takes the first 2 answers: B and C, which sit near the scanners, before A, across the yard.
How long a write waits for a yes: 2 seconds at the market. A server that can't store the write by then drops it, because the sender has stopped waiting.
A write a server threw away because it couldn't store it before the deadline. B dropped every write from 00:35 to 01:02 while compacting.
A server rewriting its stored files to free space, like rewriting a cluttered notebook onto clean pages. It makes the server slow while it runs.
Installing a newer version of a server's software. C was down for one from 00:30 to 02:00; B's is next Thursday.
How often each server passes its news on. The market's is 1 second; option 0 makes it a tenth of a second.
One interval in which every server that knows the news tells one other. News roughly doubles each round; 2 rounds reach the market's servers.
When a server gets no answer to its probe, it asks other servers to probe the silent one too, in case only its own path is broken.
How long a suspect server may stay silent before it is declared dead: 5 seconds at the market. C was declared dead at 00:30:08, 8 seconds after it stopped.
The list of servers in a group and whether each is alive, suspect or dead. Gossip keeps every server's copy of it current.
A spare server, D, rented while a home server is dead. It says yes to writes the home copies can't, and keeps a note for the dead server.
What a stand-in keeps with a write: which home server it belongs to, so it can hand it over when that server is back. Dynamo calls it a hint.
The IT firm's rule from Thursday 8 October: remove a stand-in after 30 minutes with no writes, to stop paying for it.
With no writes. D's last write was at 01:00, so it was 30 minutes idle at 01:30.
Counting only home copies' yeses, a strict quorum. A write that can't reach enough of them is refused, loudly, instead of saved on a stand-in.
A mark on a record that must never be missed, such as a recall flag. The fix counts these strictly.
A safety flag on a lot's record that makes every scanner refuse it. Ngaire set one on lot 7714 at 00:40.
What the office screen shows when a safety flag can't reach 2 home copies. The office retries every 5 minutes until it says SAVED.
A server that is in both a write's set and a read's set. The 00:40 write on A and D and the 03:15 read on B and C had none.
A regular job that compares home copies with Merkle trees and copies across whatever one lacks. The fix runs it every hour at half past.
A short fingerprint worked out from data. The same data always gives the same hash, and different data almost always a different one.
Tried, but not guaranteed. Hinted handoff is best effort: if the stand-in fails or is removed first, the note is lost.
Another word for a copy of a record kept on another server.
Another server of the same kind in the group, with no boss between them.
Data about data, like the label on a box rather than what is in it. Dynamo's hint lives in a copy's metadata.
The name a record is found by, like a cloakroom ticket. A lot number is a key.
To say yes, that a write has been stored.
Spreading news from server to server the way a cold spreads from person to person. SWIM's paper uses the word for gossip.
The part of a computer that keeps its data when it is switched off.
A control in the information security standard ISO/IEC 27001:2022, redundancy of information processing facilities: keep enough spare copies and machines that a service stays available.

atWork: Look for anything that removes servers to save money: a rule that shrinks a group of servers when it is quiet, a cleanup job that deletes idle machines, a rented machine the provider can take back. A cost rule that removes idle machines without checking what they still owe is a common pattern; it is fine for a machine that holds nothing, and dangerous for one holding writes meant for someone else. For each one, ask three things. Does anything on it hold data that has not reached its home yet, such as writes held for another server or messages waiting to be sent, and does the removal wait until that is handed over? Which records does your store count with a sloppy quorum, and which must count only their home copies? And what regular repair compares copies, how often does it run, and does anything alert when it finds differences? On a Dynamo-style store such as Cassandra, check how long its notes for down servers (its hints) are kept and how often repair runs, and test a night where a stand-in disappears. Build Night N6, Three regions that must agree, unlocks after s8e01, s8e03, s8e04 and s8e10; this case supplies its 2 of 3 quorum. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A 8.14 (redundancy of information processing facilities) expects enough spare copies to meet your availability needs; spare copies only count if they agree, so write the quorum rule for safety records and the repair schedule into the design from the first draft, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team's shopping cart service keeps each cart on 3 servers and needs 2 for a write and 2 for a read. When one of the 3 is down, a spare server takes its writes and keeps them for it. During a night of maintenance a customer's added item was confirmed, yet an hour later the two servers that answered a read didn't have it. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The write was counted on a spare, so the servers that took it and the ones the read asked shared none: R + W > N only holds among home copies
The spare's held write never reached the home server, for example because the spare was removed or failed before handing it over
Count important writes only on home copies, keep a spare until it has handed everything over, and run a regular tree repair

recall.model: The confirmation counted a spare's yes, a sloppy quorum: the write landed on one home server and the spare, and the read asked the other two home copies, so the two sets had no overlap. R + W > N only promises that among home copies. The spare should then have passed the item on, hinted handoff, but its held write was never delivered: it was removed or failed first. I'd count anything a customer is promised, like a confirmed cart item, strictly, only on home copies; keep a spare until it has handed everything over; and run a regular Merkle-tree comparison, anti-entropy, as the backstop.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with everything else as built, which one change makes the 03:15 scan show the recall without refusing any other stock write during C's upgrade?
options: Gossip every tenth of a second instead of every second
Every write and read needs all three copies
Each read asks only the nearest single copy
A safety flag counts only home copies' yeses
recall.why: Counting only home copies refuses the flag at 00:40 with A alone; the office retries and it is saved at 01:05 on A and B, so the 03:15 read on B and C finds it, and no other write is refused. Faster gossip still reads clean; all three copies refuse 17 other writes; the nearest copy, B, reads clean.

recall.prompt: A store keeps N = 3 copies of each record with W = 2 and R = 2, and counts a stand-in's yes while a home server is down. What does R + W > N still promise?
options: Every read sees the latest successful write
A read overlaps a write only among home copies
No write is ever refused while a server is down
All copies agree within one round of gossip
recall.why: Any 2 of the 3 home copies share one with any other 2, so a write that 2 home copies took is always met by a read of 2 home copies. A write counted on a stand-in falls outside that promise, as lot 7714's did. Refusing writes and gossip speed are separate matters.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: what is hinted handoff, and how do replicas find and fix differences between them?

keyIdeas.idea: A stand-in keeps a write with a note naming the home server it was meant for, and hands it over when gossip says that server is back
Anti-entropy with a Merkle tree: hashes of records, hashes of hashes; compare the top and walk down only where they differ
Handoff is best effort: a removed or failed stand-in loses its notes, so a regular comparison is the backstop

recall.model: Hinted handoff is how a stand-in covers for a down replica: it takes the write with a note saying which home server it was meant for, watches gossip for that server to come back, hands it over, and only then deletes it. It is best effort: if the stand-in fails or is removed first, the note is lost. So replicas also run anti-entropy with a Merkle tree, a summary of summaries: each record gets a hash, each branch a hash of the hashes below it. Two replicas compare the top hash; if it matches, nothing differs, and if not they walk down only the branches that differ and send just the missing records. That regular comparison is the backstop for lost notes.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Safety flags count only their home servers' yeses now, stand-ins stay until every note is handed over, and the tree repair runs every hour at half past. No recall has slipped since. Prices still use the old count. On Thursday 4 February 2027, B was down from 00:30 to 01:15 for a new disk, and C was compacting from 00:40 to 01:05, so stand-in E took writes with notes for B. At 00:50 a cut in the price of leeks was saved on A and E. At 01:10 E's own disk failed, notes and all. At 01:20 a buyer's scan of leeks read B and C and showed the old price, and he was charged it. At 01:30 the repair put the cut on B and C.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Stand-ins now stay until their notes are handed over, so why did the leek price go missing for 40 minutes, and what limits how long that can last?

keyIdeas.idea: A note lives only on the stand-in; when E's disk failed, the note went with it: hinted handoff is best effort
Prices still count a stand-in's yes, so the write on A and E shared no server with the read on B and C
The hourly tree repair is the backstop, so its interval bounds the gap; repair more often or count prices strictly

coldCase.model: The removal rule did its job; the stand-in failed instead. The note for B existed only on E, so when E's disk failed at 01:10 it went with it: hinted handoff is best effort. And prices still use the sloppy count, so the 00:50 write was counted on A and E, and the 01:20 read on B and C shared no server with it, the same no overlap as the recall night. What closed the gap was the hourly Merkle tree repair at 01:30: it is the backstop, so the repair interval bounds how long a copy can stay wrong. If an hour of a wrong price is too long, run the repair more often, or count price changes strictly, only on home copies, as the flags are.
